claims.text: A homogeneous single-phase high-entropy alloy develops localized nanoscale brittle clusters under high-strain-rate or low-temperature loading.
The nanoscale brittle clusters form through a strain-induced ordering transition.
The nanoscale brittle clusters degrade toughness by acting as internal crack-initiation sites.
The proposed HEA embrittlement mechanism is mechanistically distinct from conventional grain-boundary segregation.
The initial HEA is homogeneous and single-phase.
The initial HEA contains no pre-existing brittle clusters.
The initial HEA contains no grain-boundary segregation.
Identical high-strain-rate or cryogenic loading can activate ordering transitions without causing rapid grain growth.
High-strain-rate or low-temperature loading can provide conditions sufficient to activate local ordering in the HEA.
The relevant nanoscale ordered regions form within HEA grain interiors.
Applied mechanical loading causes local compositional fluctuations in the HEA.
Load-induced compositional fluctuations trigger nucleation of ordered nanoscale brittle clusters.
The clusters act as stress concentrators.
The loaded HEA will have lower fracture toughness than its initial state.
Under the comparison loading, conventional-alloy toughness degradation will be associated mainly with grain-boundary segregation and intermetallic precipitates.
The proposed mechanism applies while loading maintains the HEA in the single-phase region.
Prolonged thermal exposure and associated grain growth may activate alternative degradation mechanisms.

contradictions.description: The conditions specify loading that does not induce conventional grain-boundary segregation, while the predicted comparison outcome says the conventional alloy should degrade mainly through grain-boundary segregation under that loading.
